items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Except for the first time at the Jamboree, the pianist was a blind Spanish fellow named Tete Montoliu... That band really wailed.

ctx.x: The 1st of October 1962, I lost my father who had been ill for quite a while. It was as painful for Lily as it was for me. He was a great man. He was 83 years old.

For five years straight I was engaged once a year to play in the Jamboree and went twice to Madrid, once in the Whiskey club and once at the Bourbon Street. Both clubs were owned by a Frenchman named Jean-Pierre Bourbon. Except for the first time at the Jamboree, the pianist was a blind Spanish fellow named Tete Montoliu. Tete played a sort of Tatum and Bill Evans style. He had a lot of technique and like all those blind pianists had a very sensitive ear. His bass player was a German named Peter Trunk, real great…

In 1963 we decided that our flat was too small and we had sold it and taken a larger appartment in the 12th arrondissement in Paris. We had been living in the Latin Quarter for twelve years but the traffic was becoming so bad in that district and it was becoming so difficult to find parking space that we decided to leave for a less crowded part of Paris. Of course we missed the atmosphere of the Latin Quarter, the side walk cafes, the lively markets, the tourists.
